purpose: Dorzolamide is used to lower pressure inside your eye. It is prescribed for conditions like glaucoma or ocular hypertension, where the pressure in your eye is too high. Keeping eye pressure under control helps protect your vision and prevent damage to your optic nerve.
how_it_works: Your eye naturally makes a fluid called aqueous humor, which can build up and raise pressure if too much is produced. Dorzolamide works by blocking an enzyme called carbonic anhydrase, which slows down how much of this fluid your eye makes. Less fluid means lower pressure inside your eye.
common_side_effects: You may notice a brief stinging or burning feeling right after putting in the drops. Some people experience blurry vision for a short time, a bitter taste in the mouth, or mild eye redness and itching. These effects are usually temporary and not dangerous.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you are allergic to sulfa drugs, because dorzolamide is chemically related to them and may cause a similar reaction. Do not use these drops if you have severe kidney problems. Contact your doctor right away if you notice eye pain, swelling around the eye, a skin rash, or any signs of a serious allergic reaction. If you wear soft contact lenses, remove them before putting in the drops and wait at least 15 minutes before putting them back in.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is one drop in the affected eye or eyes three times a day, roughly every 8 hours. If you are using other eye drops at the same time, wait at least 10 minutes between each different drop. Always wash your hands before using and try not to let the dropper tip touch your eye or any surface.
